title: Graph Neural Networks for Accurate Quasiparticle Energy Levels in Large Supercells of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
authors: Rafael R. Del Grande, David A. Strubbe
abstract: The GW method is the one of the main workhorses of the materials science community to accurately calculate the electronic bandgap of materials, as it overcomes the gap underestimation problem from Density Functional Theory (DFT). Despite its accuracy, its computational cost becomes prohibitive when calculations have more than 10-100 atoms, which makes more difficult its use for defects, surfaces and moiré systems that demand large supercells. To overcome this problem, we developed a Graph Neural Network trained with smaller GW calculations which can make accurate predictions on large supercells at a small fraction of the computational cost. Our model uses as features the projection of DFT wavefunctions into localized atomic orbitals, while graph nodes represent the atomic positions and edges represent atom to atom distances, which captures the system geometry. We explore how to do "small AI", providing a workflow of how to create a personal and convenient dataset of GW calculations to train the model that can be applied to different materials so that the final user does not need to rely on massive datasets. We define what must be included in the training dataset to capture the physics of our objective simulation, and perform a Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters. In the case of monolayer MoS$_2$ with a sulfur vacancy our GNN models achieve high accuracy (MAE ranging 10 to 50 meV) with a simplified workflow applicable to other materials, accelerating accurate large electronic structure calculations.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural network trained on smaller GW calculations predicts quasiparticle energy levels in large MoS₂ supercells at a fraction of the computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make accurate electronic-structure calculations more accessible for large defect, surface, and moiré systems where GW is prohibitively expensive.
method: Represent atoms as graph nodes and interatomic distances as edges.
Use DFT wavefunction projections onto localized atomic orbitals as features.
Build a targeted, compact GW training dataset and tune hyperparameters with Bayesian optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: For monolayer MoS₂ with a sulfur vacancy, the abstract reports mean absolute errors of 10–50 meV for the GNN models.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to other materials or defect environments requires validation and training data that capture the relevant physics.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Neural Networks for Accurate Quasiparticle Energy Levels in Large Supercells of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides

title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
authors: Yingheng Wang, Francesco Ricci, Zhilong Wang, Tao Yu, Junwen Bai, Xiangyun Lei
abstract: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: DeepDOSReasoner predicts electronic and phonon densities of states from crystal structures while enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Millisecond-scale spectral predictions enable high-throughput materials screening without running costly DFT calculations for every candidate.
method: Map atomic structure to spectra using atom-to-energy source attention.
Refine normalized spectra through learned continuity-equation transport.
Recover element-resolved spectral contributions without direct supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model led all evaluated accuracy metrics for both spectrum types; in a prospective screen of 8,106 materials validated by new DFT calculations, 25 of its top 50 candidates were confirmed to have valence-band gaps.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the evaluated materials remains uncertain, so shortlisted candidates still warrant DFT or experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery

title: Strain-Induced Tetragonal-to-Cubic Transition in MAPbI$_3$ from Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics
authors: Daan Holleman, Luuk Klein Nagelvoort, Monica Morales-Masis, Linn Leppert
abstract: Metal-halide perovskites are promising photovoltaic absorbers whose optoelectronic properties are highly tunable. Epitaxial strain offers a route to stabilize desirable phases, tune band gaps, and reduce energetic disorder, but rational strain engineering requires predictive models. Static, zero-temperature "strained-bulk" density functional theory (DFT) calculations, successful for oxide perovskites, neglect the dynamic disorder and anharmonicity that govern halide perovskites at ambient temperature. Here, we show that molecular dynamics (MD) based on machine-learned force fields trained on-the-fly on DFT reproduces the structural and optoelectronic response of methylammonium (MA) lead iodide (MAPbI$_3$) to epitaxial strain at 300 K. We simulate bulk and free-standing slab models across experimentally accessible biaxial strains by locking the in-plane lattice vectors in nanosecond-long simulations. We predict a tetragonal-to-cubic transition at $\sim$0.5% tensile strain, marked by $c/a = 1$ and the loss of the $a^0a^0c^-$ tilting pattern, in agreement with experiments on epitaxial MAPbI$_3$ films on KCl. MA cations retain preferential orientations in the strain-induced cubic phase, unlike in its temperature-induced counterpart. Bulk and slab models yield consistent trends, with surface effects decaying within a few octahedral layers. Band gaps computed as ensemble averages over MD snapshots blue-shift under tensile strain, consistent with experiment, whereas static calculations on averaged structures predict a red shift. Our study positions MD with constrained lattice vectors as a method for predicting finite-temperature strain phase diagrams and guiding the epitaxial design of perovskite absorbers.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learned molecular dynamics predicts that about 0.5% biaxial tensile strain drives MAPbI₃ from tetragonal to cubic at 300 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Finite-temperature strain modeling can guide epitaxial perovskite design to stabilize target phases and tune photovoltaic absorber band gaps.
method: Train machine-learned force fields on-the-fly using DFT.
Run nanosecond bulk and free-standing slab simulations with fixed in-plane lattice vectors.
Track lattice symmetry, octahedral tilts, molecular orientations, and snapshot-averaged band gaps.
infographic.evidence_signal: The predicted transition agrees with MAPbI₃-on-KCl experiments, while snapshot-averaged band gaps reproduce the experimental tensile-strain blue shift that static averaged structures miss.
infographic.watch_item: Free-standing slabs do not explicitly capture substrate interfaces, so interface-specific effects require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-Induced Tetragonal-to-Cubic Transition in MAPbI$_3$ from Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics

title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
authors: Changzhi Ai, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation across various material surfaces.

infographic.key_insight: AdsNet predicts adsorption energies directly from local atomic graphs, combining geometric sensitivity with computation that does not scale with total system size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could accelerate catalyst screening and local interface relaxation without evaluating full-system machine-learning potentials.
method: Build a cutoff-based graph of adsorbate atoms and their immediate surface neighbors.
Use equivariant message passing with scalar and vector features to predict adsorption energy and per-atom contributions.
Obtain analytic forces through automatic differentiation for projected-gradient relaxation with adaptive line search.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 33,920 DFT structures spanning 26 transition metals and six adsorbates, AdsNet reports an energy RMSE of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/Å.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization to unseen surface chemistries or environments where interactions beyond the local cutoff matter.
infographic.paper_title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction

title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys
authors: Xiang Meng, Shuhei Shinzato, Zhiqiang Zhao, Linfeng Yu, Jian Guo, Liangli Chu
abstract: Boron (B) microalloying can effectively refine microstructures of as-cast TiAl alloys and regulate their mechanical properties. Yet, how dilute B exists in TiAl and interacts with defects and how these interactions govern high-temperature deformation remain elusive. Here, we systematically elucidate defect-mediated B redistribution in TiAl alloys and its consequences for their deformation using hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations augmented with a newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning potential. As a typical product of B microalloying, borides are markedly stiffer than the TiAl matrix and act as brittle reinforcing phases, while borides/matrix interfacial adhesion depends on surface termination and stacking sequence. In the bulk, interstitial B tends to be trapped at Ti-rich octahedral sites by high migration barriers but can kinetically evolve into substitutional dopants upon approaching Al vacancies. Increased tensile stress and vacancy concentration further promote B enrichment in the bulk. B is enriched at semi-coherent $γ/α_2$ boundaries and preferentially partitions into the $α_2$ phase. In polycrystalline TiAl, B accumulates primarily in disordered regions, raising the average flow stress by 9.4% at 1 at.% B and 900 K. This strengthening is accompanied by reduced shear strain accumulation. Simulated microstructural evolution and stacking-fault energetics indicate that B impedes dislocation glide via local pinning and suppresses deformation twinning, thereby increasing resistance to plastic deformation. By linking solute redistribution to defect interactions and deformation, these findings establish an atomistic framework for understanding and designing high-performance alloys based on interstitial solutes.

infographic.key_insight: Boron redistributes toward defects in TiAl alloys, locally pinning dislocations and suppressing deformation twinning to increase high-temperature strength.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling boron content and defect structure could help strengthen TiAl alloys, while accounting for brittle borides and termination-dependent interface adhesion.
method: Hybrid grand-canonical Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations
Newly developed high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential
Atomistic analysis of boron partitioning, defect interactions, and deformation
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulated polycrystalline TiAl at 900 K, 1 at.% boron increased average flow stress by 9.4% and reduced shear strain accumulation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported strengthening is simulation-based; experimental validation and transferability across alloy compositions and loading conditions remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Atomistic insight into defect-mediated boron redistribution and high-temperature strengthening in TiAl alloys

title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
authors: Harry Sevi, Joonatan E. M. Laulainen
abstract: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

infographic.key_insight: Better reliability diagnostics do not necessarily improve materials screening decisions or reduce DFT verification costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate reliability interventions by how much DFT they avoid while preserving required recall of near-hull candidates, rather than by prediction metrics alone.
method: Rank candidate crystal structures with MACE-MP, CHGNet, and Orb V3 before DFT verification.
Test novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits against the screening objective.
Use two-oracle analysis to distinguish misaligned reliability targets from finite-budget audit limitations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the three interventions, improvements in immediate diagnostic targets did not consistently translate into better downstream screening decisions.
infographic.watch_item: Routing benefits depend on the screening objective: perfect average-ranking information can still select the wrong model under formation-energy screening, while finite-budget audits limit gains in the evaluated hull-aligned variant.
infographic.paper_title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery

title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
authors: Yanlin Fei, Lei Li, Shaolong Chen, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, Madalina Ciobanu
abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

infographic.key_insight: MatHarness supports open-ended computational materials research from ideation to manuscript by combining robust execution, evolving scientific reasoning, and multi-agent review.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The harness offers a framework for coordinating long-running simulation campaigns while retaining human approval and strategic oversight.
method: Pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing improve execution robustness.
Persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model support plan revision.
A heterogeneous multi-agent round table operates under targeted human oversight.

infographic.watch_item: Evidence comes from one research campaign, and its materials conclusions are limited to sampled metallic dilute-limit models with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions.
infographic.paper_title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science

title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation
authors: Ruiqi Dong, Haotian Huang, Yubin Hu, Guixiang Zeng
abstract: Conventional two-stage distillation first establishes a teacher through teacher-driven configuration exploration, a costly first stage for complex materials, and then uses its predictions to supervise students, potentially propagating teacher-label errors. Here, we propose distillation-driven teacher-student co-evolution (DICE), which uses a fast student to accelerate configuration exploration and replaces the fixed teacher-to-student sequence with alternating student and teacher updates. A representation-based support-assessment algorithm routes high-support configurations to teacher labelling and selects low-support configurations for density functional theory (DFT) calculations to update the teacher, thereby reducing the risk of teacher-label error propagation to students. Across Al2O3 (structural ceramics), yttria-stabilised zirconia (solid electrolytes) and MIL-120(Al) (a metal-organic framework), DICE develops reliable compact potentials using only 140-494 target DFT reference configurations per system; total recorded student exploration times per system are just 2.6-5.1% of the corresponding teacher-driven estimates. Combining computational efficiency with broad applicability across diverse material systems, DICE provides a practical route to developing reliable compact interatomic potentials.

infographic.key_insight: DICE co-evolves teacher and student interatomic potentials, using fast student-driven exploration and reliability-aware labelling to reduce development cost and teacher-error propagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a more efficient route to compact interatomic potentials for simulations of ceramics, solid electrolytes and metal–organic frameworks.
method: Use a fast student potential to explore atomic configurations.
Route high-support configurations to teacher labelling and low-support configurations to DFT using representation-based support assessment.
Alternate teacher and student updates rather than following a fixed two-stage distillation sequence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Al2O3, yttria-stabilised zirconia and MIL-120(Al), DICE used 140–494 target DFT reference configurations per system, with recorded student exploration times at 2.6–5.1% of corresponding teacher-driven estimates.
infographic.watch_item: Support assessment must reliably flag unfamiliar configurations; exploration-time savings alone do not establish equivalent reductions in total development cost.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation

title: Prediction and characterisation of cation topology of pentanary high-entropy alloy (MoWNbTaV)S$_2$
authors: Shubham Agarwal, Tahir Wahab, Jesper Byggmästar, Antonio Cammarata, Tomas Polcar
abstract: High-entropy transition-metal dichalcogenides offer properties tuned by composition, yet two basic questions remain open: which arrangement of the metals forms under synthesis conditions, and how it can be recognised in experiment. Density functional theory (DFT) cannot sample the vast space of possible arrangements, and the ground-state energies usually employed to screen them do not take into account the temperatures at which these materials are made. This work solves both issues for the pentanary (MoWNbTaV)S\textsubscript{2} monolayer with a Gaussian approximation potential trained on DFT data by iterative learning. Gibbs free energy calculations reveal that vibrational entropy reshapes the stability ranking, while five selected configurations retain their trigonal-prismatic framework during nanosecond molecular dynamics up to \qty{1300}{\kelvin}. Raman and infrared spectra combine parent-monolayer signatures with disorder-activated modes, providing fingerprints for experimental identification. % The predicted lattice parameter follows Vegard's law and agrees within \qty{0.8}{\percent} with X{-}ray diffraction on a sputtered alloy film, which identifies the solid solution but not the arrangement of its metals: distinguishing between arrangements requires the vibrational fingerprints. The potential and its development workflow enable further atomistic simulations and offer a transferable approach to screening related two-dimensional high-entropy materials.

infographic.key_insight: An AI interatomic potential enables cation-arrangement screening in (MoWNbTaV)S₂, revealing that vibrational entropy changes stability rankings and vibrational spectra provide fingerprints for identification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports finite-temperature screening and experimental characterisation of two-dimensional high-entropy materials beyond practical DFT sampling limits.
method: Train a Gaussian approximation potential on DFT data through iterative learning.
Calculate Gibbs free energies and run nanosecond molecular dynamics.
Analyse Raman and infrared spectra for configuration-sensitive signatures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Five selected configurations retained their trigonal-prismatic framework during nanosecond simulations up to 1300 K, while free-energy calculations showed entropy-driven changes in stability rankings.
infographic.watch_item: Simulated stability of selected configurations does not establish which cation arrangement forms during synthesis; experimental validation of the predicted fingerprints remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Prediction and characterisation of cation topology of pentanary high-entropy alloy (MoWNbTaV)S$_2$

title: Interface-Engineered Piezoelectricity and Electromechanical Coupling in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures
authors: Shivanand Yadav, Raihan Ahammed, Umer Ali, B. S. Bhadoria, Yogesh S. Chauhan, Amit Agarwal
abstract: Interfaces between dissimilar two-dimensional (2D) materials provide a route to engineer electromechanical responses that are not intrinsic to the individual constituent layers. Here, we use high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate 461 van der Waals heterostructures constructed from 57 2D monolayers and establish a materials-design framework linking work-function mismatch, interfacial charge redistribution, dipole formation, and strain-dependent electromechanical response. We find that heterostructure formation generates out-of-plane interfacial dipoles via charge redistribution between the constituent layers, while biaxial in-plane strain systematically modulates them. The resulting heterostructures exhibit two distinct regimes: metallic interfaces with strain-tunable interfacial dipoles and semiconducting heterostructures with well-defined piezoelectric responses. For the latter, Berry-phase (BP) calculations independently validate the charge-density-difference (CDD) approach, which is generally applicable to all representative systems, with piezoelectric coefficients calculated via two methods agreeing to within 10%. Among 24 selected heterostructures, effective biaxial interfacial electromechanical coefficients reach 83.35 pCm-1 . These results demonstrate that the interface can serve as the active element governing electromechanical coupling and provide a computationally guided strategy for designing strain-tunable out-of-plane electromechanical responses in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

infographic.key_insight: Interfaces between dissimilar 2D materials generate out-of-plane dipoles that can be tuned by in-plane strain, enabling interface-engineered electromechanical coupling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Work-function mismatch and interfacial charge redistribution offer design guides for strain-tunable electromechanical components based on van der Waals heterostructures.
method: Screened 461 heterostructures assembled from 57 monolayers using high-throughput DFT.
Linked work-function mismatch, charge redistribution, and interfacial dipoles under biaxial strain.
Compared charge-density-difference and Berry-phase calculations for semiconducting heterostructures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 24 selected heterostructures, effective biaxial interfacial electromechanical coefficients reached 83.35 pC/m; the two calculation methods agreed within 10% for semiconducting systems.
infographic.watch_item: Results are computational; metallic interfaces show strain-tunable dipoles rather than the well-defined piezoelectric response identified in semiconducting systems.
infographic.paper_title: Interface-Engineered Piezoelectricity and Electromechanical Coupling in Two-Dimensional van der Waals Heterostructures

title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves
authors: Yuan Xu, Maxim V. Shugaev, Leonid V. Zhigilei
abstract: Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are widely used to probe near-surface material properties and microstructure, but their potential to drive permanent structural modification remains largely unexplored. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations reveal the mechanisms of defect generation and evolution induced by nonlinear Rayleigh waves in Pt. Strong crystallographic dependence of the nonlinear evolution is observed. SAWs on Pt(111) undergo rapid nonlinear sharpening and shock formation, with localized elastic energy and increasing near-surface stresses, whereas much weaker sharpening on Pt(001) allows dissipation to compete effectively with shock formation. For sufficiently strong SAWs on Pt(111), Shockley partial dislocations are emitted from the surface when the resolved shear stress approaches the theoretical shear strength. The highly localized and rapidly changing stress field at the shock front activates multiple slip systems and promotes crossslip and reactions between Shockley partials, producing complex dislocation structures with sessile stair-rod segments. Subsequent SAW interactions activate dislocation sources on slip systems where the stress is insufficient for homogeneous nucleation, leading, in one case, to sequential emission of Shockley partials and formation of a subsurface twinned domain. Repeated SAW passages progressively reduce dislocation density, demonstrating SAW-driven nonthermal annealing. Dislocation interactions with the free surface generate atomic-scale steps, terraces, and other under-coordinated configurations, providing a microscopic pathway for permanent surface modification that may contribute to the acoustically enhanced catalytic activity observed on Pt surfaces. These results establish nonlinear SAWs as drivers of nonthermal defect generation, restructuring, and annealing, opening opportunities for acoustic processing of near-surface microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlinear surface acoustic waves can generate, restructure, and nonthermally anneal near-surface dislocations in platinum while creating permanent atomic-scale roughness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Acoustic processing could enable control of platinum’s near-surface microstructure and surface morphology, with potential relevance to catalysis.
method: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of nonlinear Rayleigh waves in platinum.
Comparison of wave sharpening and dissipation on Pt(111) and Pt(001).
Tracking dislocation nucleation, reactions, and surface changes across repeated wave passages.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show rapid shock formation on Pt(111), Shockley partial emission near the theoretical shear strength, and progressive dislocation-density reduction under repeated wave passages.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are simulation-based and strongly orientation-dependent; experimental processing conditions and catalytic benefits remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves

title: Altermagnetism of MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 in a wurtzite-based crystal structure
authors: Ilteris K. Turan, Jonathan Agrinya, Walter R. L. Lambrecht
abstract: Based on symmetry analysis, the Pna2_1 wurtzite-based crystal structure with Mn as a magnetic group-II element, MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 belong to the class of altermagnets because spin-up and spin-down Mn in the unit cell are related by rotation or mirror plane type operations rather than inversion or translation. Spin polarized density functional theory calculations and quasiparticle self-consistent (QS) GW calculations support the symmetry analysis and identify the lowest-energy spin configuration as Pna'2_1' in agreement with neutron diffraction data. The altermagnetic band splittings allowed for the three different antiferromagnetic ordering patterns are reported and symmetry analyzed. Additionally, spin wave dispersions, chiral magnon spltting, and Neel temperature estimates from the mean-field and random-phase approximations are provided, as well as calculations of the optical dielectric function using the Bethe-Salpeter Equation method. MnSiN2 exhibits both Wannier-type excitons with N-p to Si-s transition character and charge-transfer Frenkel-type excitons with hole on N-p and electron on Mn-d orbital character.

infographic.key_insight: MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 in the wurtzite-based Pna2_1 structure are predicted altermagnets, with opposite-spin Mn sites related by rotations or mirrors rather than inversion or translation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These compounds offer candidate materials for exploring spin-dependent electronic, magnonic, and optical responses in altermagnetic devices.
method: Crystal and magnetic symmetry analysis
Spin-polarized DFT and quasiparticle self-consistent GW calculations
Spin-wave modeling and Bethe–Salpeter optical calculations
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations identify Pna′2_1′ as the lowest-energy spin configuration, consistent with neutron diffraction, and predict spin-dependent band splittings and chiral magnon splitting.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report experimental validation of the predicted band splittings, magnon chirality, or excitonic responses.
infographic.paper_title: Altermagnetism of MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 in a wurtzite-based crystal structure

title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system
authors: Aljoscha Felix Baumann, Reyhaneh Ghassemizadeh, Daniel F. Urban
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically. Using density functional theory (DFT), we compute rigid-body separation (RBS) curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni GBs, extracting the work of separation $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and maximum traction $σ_{\max}$ via the universal binding energy relation (UBER). We find that substitution of Cr or Fe into the GB plane increases both quantities relative to pure Ni GBs. To overcome the size limitations of DFT, we compare several machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) foundation models against the DFT dataset and identify a model achieving quantitative agreement with DFT for $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $σ_{\max}$. This MLIP enables systematic sampling of alloying configurations at finer concentration steps. We show that alloying-induced changes in GB cohesion depend on both, element type and local structures, revealing trends that are inaccessible with DFT alone. Extending the analysis to a ternary $\mathrm{Ni}_{56}\mathrm{Fe}_{20}\mathrm{Cr}_{24}$ composition, inspired by the principal constituents of the widely used commercial Alloy 718, shows that the binary trends provide a useful basis for interpreting the combined effect of both substitutes, while explicit ternary calculations are required to capture their interplay quantitatively. Together, these results provide a validated workflow for quantifying the effect of alloying elements on GB cohesion in multicomponent alloys. The resulting values may serve as input for continuum-scale fracture models, paving the way toward atomistically informed multiscale modeling.

infographic.key_insight: Fe or Cr substitution at Ni grain boundaries increases cohesion, with gains depending on element type and local atomic structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Validated atomistic cohesion predictions can supply inputs for continuum fracture models of multicomponent Ni-based alloys.
method: Compute DFT rigid-body separation curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni grain boundaries.
Extract work of separation and maximum traction using the universal binding energy relation.
Benchmark ML interatomic potentials against DFT, then use a validated model to sample binary and ternary alloy configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: One tested ML potential quantitatively reproduced DFT work of separation and maximum traction, enabling finer concentration sampling and analysis of Ni56Fe20Cr24.
infographic.watch_item: Binary alloying trends do not quantitatively capture Fe–Cr interplay; explicit ternary calculations remain necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system

title: Solute-Aware Stochastic Korhonen Model of Electromigration in Wide vs Near-Bamboo Al-Cu Lines
authors: Narahara Chari Dingari, David R. Heskett
abstract: We couple an evolving Cu field to the one-dimensional Korhonen stress equation on random grain maps for wide (10 $μ$m), narrow (3 $μ$m) and near-bamboo Al-Cu lines. Earlier random-microstructure simulations fixed the Cu effect, and most continuum solute models used prescribed structures with all Cu mobile; we join the two and let only dissolved Cu move, the excess staying as immobile precipitate. With $10^3$ maps per condition at 200 $^\circ$C, we report nucleation times and sites, immortal fractions and Black's-law parameters. In cathode-limited lines Cu depletion shortens the median nucleation time 1.15- to 1.20-fold relative to immobile Cu for the cited Cu diffusivity; treating all Cu as mobile overstates this a further 2.24- to 2.36-fold at 2 wt%; the exponent stays near 2. In wide lines with reservoir ends, Cu steps left by the immobile precipitate become the failure sites, removing their Cu-free immortality if a quarter or more of the precipitate blocks Al diffusion. With Cu above the solvus the lifetime is not Arrhenius, as the dissolved fraction rises with temperature: a Black's-law fit at 250 to 300 $^\circ$C overestimates the median nucleation time at 150 $^\circ$C up to 2.33-fold at 2 wt% Cu with an exponent near 2. At the test durations the model qualitatively matches the cathode-side damage in narrow lines and the Cu build-up and mid-line peaks in wide lines but not the cathode-side Cu peaks or longer lives of narrow lines.

infographic.key_insight: Coupling mobile dissolved Cu with immobile precipitates reveals that Cu depletion and precipitate-induced transport barriers can accelerate electromigration failure and invalidate simple Arrhenius lifetime extrapolation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Al–Cu interconnect reliability predictions should account for Cu solubility, precipitate blocking, microstructure and end conditions rather than treating all Cu as mobile.
method: Couple an evolving Cu field to the one-dimensional Korhonen stress equation.
Simulate random grain maps for wide (10 μm), narrow (3 μm) and near-bamboo lines.
Track nucleation times and sites, immortal fractions and Black’s-law parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 1,000 grain maps per condition at 200 °C, the model predicts 1.15–1.20-fold shorter median nucleation times with Cu depletion than with immobile Cu; separate temperature analysis finds high-temperature fits can overestimate lifetime at 150 °C by up to 2.33-fold.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement is qualitative: the model does not reproduce cathode-side Cu peaks or the longer lifetimes observed in narrow lines.
infographic.paper_title: Solute-Aware Stochastic Korhonen Model of Electromigration in Wide vs Near-Bamboo Al-Cu Lines

title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling
authors: Haoan Xu, Ruike Chen, Jing Xia, Haotian Li, Huanyun Zhang, Cong Sun
abstract: Fetal brain diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a pivotal non-invasive tool for assessing the development of brain connectivity and microstructure. However, the prolonged acquisition times and complex sampling requirements render dMRI highly susceptible to unpredictable fetal motion. Existing motion correction methods typically process each dMRI volume independently and focus on inter-slice motion. Such strategies fail to utilize the coherent information between dMRI volumes along different diffusion directions and lack the ability to restore the intra-slice corruption. To address these limitations, we proposed iFeST, an iterative framework that combines frequency (k-space), spatial, and temporal (inter-slice) modeling for fetal brain dMRI motion correction. At each iteration, iFeST integrates information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs). These distributions encode local fiber orientations within each voxel and serve as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment in the next iteration. To train the framework, we developed a fetal brain dMRI motion simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs. Evaluation on simulated datasets demonstrated that iFeST outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in image restoration. Further validation on a real-world dataset confirmed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines. Overall, iFeST provides a learning-based framework for fetal dMRI motion correction, restoring motion-corrupted data and improving microstructural reconstruction for downstream diagnostic applications.

infographic.key_insight: iFeST iteratively combines frequency, spatial, and temporal modeling to correct fetal brain diffusion MRI motion and improve microstructural reconstruction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This medical-imaging framework, rather than a materials-science method, addresses both within-slice corruption and between-slice misalignment.
method: Integrate information across diffusion directions into fiber orientation distributions (FODs).
Use FODs as microstructural priors for intra-slice restoration and inter-slice alignment at the next iteration.
Train using a fetal brain dMRI simulator that synthesizes compound motion artifacts from FODs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulated evaluations outperformed four inter-slice networks in motion estimation and three intra-slice networks in restoration; real-world validation showed significantly better volume reconstruction and FOD estimation than conventional pipelines.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization across scanners and acquisition protocols remains unclear from the abstract, which provides no dataset sizes or numerical effect sizes.
infographic.paper_title: iFeST: An Iterative Motion Correction Framework for Fetal Brain Diffusion MRI via Frequency-Spatial-Temporal Modeling

title: Nonmonotonic In-Plane Thermal Transport in Metal-Embedded Graphitic Carbon Nitride
authors: Wenwu Jiang, Hekai Bu, Wei Qiu, Yong Ni
abstract: Embedding metal atoms within the intrinsic cavities of graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) modifies its local bonding and vibrational properties, yet its consequences for lattice thermal transport remain poorly understood. Here, we combine a machine-learned potential (MLP) with homogeneous nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) to investigate in-plane thermal transport in Cu-embedded g-C3N4 across the full range of cavity occupation. The thermal conductivity exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on Cu occupation, decreasing at intermediate occupation and partially recovering as the cavities approach full occupation. Frequency-resolved analysis reveals that this behavior originates from the competition between two phonon contributions. The low-frequency vibrations introduced by Cu couple to the intrinsic modes of g-C3N4, reconstructing the phonon dispersion and suppressing thermal transport below 10 THz. With increasing Cu occupation, the collective mechanical response of the N atoms surrounding the cavities is enhanced, accompanied by increased phonon group velocities in the 20-30 THz range and a corresponding recovery of the high-frequency thermal contribution. The competition between the saturating low-frequency suppression and the increasing high-frequency contribution gives rise to the nonmonotonic thermal conductivity. A similar occupation dependence and spectral redistribution are observed for Ag-embedded g-C3N4. These results identify competing phonon contributions as the microscopic origin of nonmonotonic thermal transport in metal-embedded g-C3N4 and suggest that occupation of intrinsic cavities provides a route to redistributing phonon transport in porous crystalline materials.

infographic.key_insight: Thermal conductivity in Cu-embedded g-C3N4 falls at intermediate cavity occupation and partially recovers near full occupation because low- and high-frequency phonon contributions compete.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling metal occupation of intrinsic cavities offers a potential route to tuning in-plane heat transport in porous crystalline materials.
method: Machine-learned interatomic potential
Homogeneous nonequilibrium molecular dynamics across cavity occupations
Frequency-resolved thermal transport analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show suppressed transport below 10 THz and a recovering contribution at 20–30 THz as Cu occupation increases, with similar trends for Ag.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation results but no experimental validation of the occupation-dependent thermal response.
infographic.paper_title: Nonmonotonic In-Plane Thermal Transport in Metal-Embedded Graphitic Carbon Nitride

title: Weight Averaging at Small Budgets Confounds Formula-Labeled Pretraining in Microstructure-Property Regression: A Pre-Specified Study with Post Hoc Rechecks
authors: Jonghyun Lee, Soojung Kang
abstract: Closed-form physics formulas can label synthetic microstructures at no cost, so supervised pretraining on those labels is an alternative to self-supervised pretraining when labels are scarce. One pre-specified protocol tests this on two public simulated benchmarks, two-phase conductivity and short-fiber stiffness: a ConvNeXt-Small is pretrained on 150,000 synthetic images by formula regression or masked reconstruction and fine-tuned on 100, 400, or 1,600 labels. Five fine-tuning seeds from one formula checkpoint have mean residual correlations of 0.994 (conductivity) and 0.999 (stiffness). On conductivity the formula network compresses its predictions (slope 0.64) and has four times the 400-label error of ImageNet initialization. Two confounds interact: the generator renders the low-conductivity phase with the opposite contrast polarity, and the exponential moving average (EMA; decay 0.995, no bias correction) still holds 16% of the initial weights after the 400-label schedule. Without the EMA the slope is 0.97, and over three subsets and five seeds the mismatched checkpoint has 1.4 times the ImageNet error (0.0119 versus 0.0084). Three pretraining runs per polarity leave the comparison inconclusive: matched means (0.0086, 0.0111, 0.0118) fall below mismatched means (0.0119, 0.0120, 0.0123) in aggregate (0.0105 versus 0.0121) but overlap on two of three subsets, and the matched spread (0.0032) exceeds the mismatched spread (0.0004). On stiffness without the EMA, formula pretraining lowers the 100-label error by 18% versus ImageNet over five seeds, including a re-initialized head, while ImageNet seeds also correlate at 0.992. Weight averages that start at the pretrained weights can dominate small-budget comparisons and should be rechecked at the last weights.

infographic.key_insight: At small fine-tuning budgets, EMA anchored to pretrained weights can confound formula-pretraining comparisons, making last-weight evaluation essential.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For label-scarce microstructure-property prediction, audit weight averaging and image contrast conventions before choosing a pretraining strategy.
method: Pretrain ConvNeXt-Small on 150,000 synthetic images using formula regression or masked reconstruction.
Fine-tune conductivity and short-fiber stiffness models with 100, 400, or 1,600 labels.
Recheck results without EMA and test matched versus mismatched phase contrast.
infographic.evidence_signal: Without EMA, conductivity formula pretraining had 1.4× ImageNet error across three subsets and five seeds, while stiffness formula pretraining reduced 100-label error by 18% over five seeds.
infographic.watch_item: Post hoc contrast-polarity rechecks remained inconclusive across three pretraining runs per polarity, so they do not establish a robust benefit from correcting contrast.
infographic.paper_title: Weight Averaging at Small Budgets Confounds Formula-Labeled Pretraining in Microstructure-Property Regression: A Pre-Specified Study with Post Hoc Rechecks

title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations
authors: Cao Thang Nguyen, Sung Youb Kim
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer an efficient paradigm for large-scale atomistic simulations with near first-principles accuracy. However, developing and deploying these potentials often involves intricate procedures that require substantial manual effort and domain expertise. In this work, we present CLFF, an open-source Python framework designed to automate concurrent learning workflows for MLIPs. CLFF integrates model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based candidate selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation into a unified workflow. The framework currently supports several modern graph-based MLIP architectures and is compatible with widely used computational chemistry and materials science tools. A distinguishing feature of CLFF is its ability to asynchronously distribute computational tasks across multiple heterogeneous remote computing resources, enabling users to aggregate fragmented hardware infrastructure within a single controllable workflow. In addition to concurrent learning, CLFF provides automated workflows for initial data generation and material property calculations, including phonon dispersion and potential energy surface scans. By minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility, CLFF offers a flexible platform for developing and deploying MLIPs in computational materials research.

infographic.key_insight: CLFF automates concurrent learning for machine-learning interatomic potentials, unifying model development and deployment in an open-source Python framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It reduces manual workflow coordination and pools heterogeneous remote computing resources for atomistic simulations and material property calculations.
method: Integrate model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation.
Distribute computational tasks asynchronously across multiple heterogeneous remote resources.
Automate initial data generation, phonon dispersion calculations, and potential energy surface scans.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes workflow capabilities and support for several graph-based MLIP architectures but reports no quantitative accuracy, speedup, or validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Compatibility and resource coordination should be verified for the intended models, simulation tools, and remote computing environments.
infographic.paper_title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures
authors: Xin Qian, Te-Huan Liu, Xiaobo Li, Ronggui Yang
abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.

infographic.key_insight: This review highlights how AI-assisted thermoreflectance imaging can help map nanoscale thermal properties and reveal heat transport shaped by interfaces and defects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved local thermal characterization could support materials discovery and thermal management in heterogeneous electronics and advanced manufacturing.
method: Use non-contact pump–probe thermoreflectance with wide-field imaging or scanning.
Apply AI-assisted processing to thermal-property mapping and interfacial transport visualization.
Explore nonintrusive subsurface characterization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract summarizes recent advances but reports no datasets, quantitative accuracy metrics, or benchmark comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Imaging throughput must be balanced against measurement accuracy and confidence in extracting multiple thermal parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

title: Transition-Metal Substitutions in MOF-5: A Hybrid-DFT Study of Oxygen Electrocatalysis
authors: Pedro H. Souza, Walter Orellana
abstract: Hybrid density functional theory calculations were used to investigate the stability, electronic properties, and catalytic activity of transition-metal impurities substituting Zn sites (M\(_{\rm Zn}\)) in the MOF-5 metal-organic framework [Zn\(_4\)O(BDC)\(_3\), BDC = 1,4-benzenedicarboxylate], with M = Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu. Most substitutions introduce \(3d\) states within the MOF-5 band gap and induce localized magnetic moments. Partially occupied \(3d\) states promote orbital hybridization and charge transfer with oxygenated intermediates, activating the dopant sites toward oxygen electrocatalysis. The oxygen reduction and evolution reaction (ORR and OER) activities were evaluated using the computational hydrogen electrode model. Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Fe\(_{\rm Zn}\) exhibit calculated ORR overpotentials of 0.57~V, while Mn\(_{\rm Zn}\) and Co\(_{\rm Zn}\) yield OER overpotentials of 0.42 and 0.51~V, respectively, approaching those of benchmark precious-metal electrocatalysts. These findings identify Mn substitution as a promising strategy for achieving bifunctional ORR/OER activity in MOF-5 and establish a link between dopant electronic structure and catalytic performance to guide the design of MOF-based electrocatalysts.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid-DFT calculations identify Mn-substituted MOF-5 as a promising bifunctional oxygen electrocatalyst, linking dopant electronic structure to ORR/OER activity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Replacing selected Zn sites with transition metals offers a computationally guided route to MOF-based catalysts with reduced reliance on precious metals.
method: Model Sc–Cu substitutions at Zn sites in MOF-5 using hybrid DFT.
Assess stability, electronic structure, and interactions with oxygenated intermediates.
Estimate ORR/OER overpotentials using the computational hydrogen electrode model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculated ORR overpotentials are 0.57 V for Mn and Fe substitutions; OER overpotentials are 0.42 V for Mn and 0.51 V for Co substitutions.
infographic.watch_item: These computational predictions require experimental validation of dopant incorporation, catalytic activity, and framework durability under operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Transition-Metal Substitutions in MOF-5: A Hybrid-DFT Study of Oxygen Electrocatalysis
